More recently the PRT concept was captured by the term automated transit network (ATN), which encompasses the service concept of PRT but is more encompassing of various technologies, even including AV fleets on public rights-of-way. An ATN system is formally defined in the ANSI/ASCE 21-21 Automated People Mover Standards. At its core, whether PRT, ATN, or ODT, these services use a network for optimized routing to service individuals, parties, or small groups as opposed to a predefined operating route with fixed stations. The complexity of dispatching each individual vehicle to serve an individual travel party with a point-to-point ride on an optimized travel path requires a substantially more complex vehicle dispatching control system when performed in real time. As a result, it has been only in the last 25 years that fixed-guideway ATN systems comprising a fleet of small vehicles have been implemented at a few districts around the world. The study and simulation of several proposed ATN systems over the past 20 years provides significant parallel insight with respect to incorporating ODT service within an AMD. A review 41 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. of select ATN simulation studies in the next edition to follow in the report series reveals the criticality of appropriate station design incorporating offline and parallel berths for maximum throughput and resiliency, the importance of pre-positioning vehicles in anticipation of peak periods of demand, and having adequate vehicles and vehicle storage to service surge flows at high-demand stations such as an intermodal station connecting an AMD to high-capacity regional and interregional transit. The nondeterministic nature of ODT also makes recharging EVs more challenging, calling for better integration of charging into stations using locations where the vehicles naturally dwell, providing the best opportunity for battery charging. 4.2 Fleet Management and the Operational Control System With the maturing of ADS, attention is now turning to the management of AV fleets for the provision of public mobility. With the human driver removed from these vehicles, several aspects of fleet management must be rethought. In some cases, the absence of a driver provides additional fleet-level benefits in terms of flexibility and scheduling; in other cases, it presents challenges—particularly with respect to unexpected situations (outside the operational design domain) and communicating with riders. This section of research draws on parallels from automated guideway transit fleet management in which communications-based train control allows fully automated operations. The NLR AMD research uses “automated supervisory and dispatch control” (ASDC) as developed in a 2021 SAE International conference paper (Lott, Young, and Zhu 2021) to refer to the fleet management of AVs. It has analogies and parallels to communications-based train control principles of operation but applied to fleets of AVs for public mobility.
